paper_title: MAGPIE: Agentic Multi-Reference Image Generation via Executable Scene Construction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multi-reference image generation requires a model to preserve the appearance of selected subjects while arranging them according to an instruction. Despite recent progress in reference-based generation and compositional control, reliably organizing selected subjects into the intended scene remains challenging. Although existing methods provide various forms of compositional guidance, the planned relationships are not always explicitly instantiated for inspection and refinement before image synthesis. To address this limitation, we introduce MAGPIE, which represents the intended composition as a simplified 3D scene defined by an executable Blender program. A coding agent links each scene instance to its reference, checks the geometry and rendered view against the instruction, and revises the program to correct discrepancies. The final proxy rendering serves as a visual plan for the image generator. Using MAGPIE-Instruct-3K, we train the generator to follow this plan while drawing each subject's appearance from its reference. MAGPIE improves both Qwen and FLUX on DreamOmni2 and SconeEval. With FLUX, it improves overall success on DreamOmni2 by 28.21 percentage points over the original backbone and achieves the highest overall score among the models evaluated on SconeEval.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multi-reference image generation requires model to preserve the appearance of selected subjects while arranging them according to an instruction. Despite recent progress in reference-based generation and compositional control, reliably organizing selected subjects into the intended scene remains challenging. Although existing methods provide various forms of compositional guidance, the planned relationships are not always explicitly instantiated for inspection and refinement before image synthesis. To address this limitation, we introduce MAGPIE, which represents the intended composition as simplified 3D scene defined by an executable Blender program. coding agent links each scene instance to its reference, checks the geometry and rendered view against the instruction, and revises the program to correct discrepancies. The final proxy rendering serves as visual plan for the image generator. Using MAGPIE-Instruct-3K, we train the generator to follow this plan while drawing each subjects appearance from its reference. MAGPIE improves both Qwen and FLUX on DreamOmni2 and SconeEval. With FLUX, it improves overall success on DreamOmni2 by 28.21 percentage points over the original backbone and achieves the highest overall score among the models evaluated on SconeEval. 1. Introduction Multi-reference image generation (MRIG) enables users to compose personalized images from heterogeneous visual references and natural language instructions [12, 30, 32, 33, 35, 36]. Recent advances have improved reference fidelity and instruction understanding: DreamOmni2 [35] supports multimodal generation and editing, while Scone [30] explicitly addresses subject selection among multiple candi- *These authors contributed equally to this work. 1 Figure 1. Comparison of representative existing methods and MAGPIE. (a) Existing methods provide semantic or spatial guidance without necessarily exposing an explicit scene for verification. (b) In contrast, MAGPIE instantiates compositional intent as an executable 3D proxy, enabling revision before referencegrounded appearance synthesis. dates. However, faithfully preserving the appearance of referenced subjects does not necessarily ensure that they are composed correctly [18, 30]. As instructions require selective inclusion, multiple instances, and interactions among subjects, the generator must organize them into scene that satisfies the requested spatial and interaction relationships. This difficulty motivates closer look at how directgeneration pipelines organize scene [33, 35, 36], as illustrated in Fig. 1(a). Within this paradigm, generative model must implicitly determine which entities should appear and how they should be organized while simultaneously synthesizing their reference-specific appearances. Without an explicit intermediate scene, compositional errors such as missing instance or an incorrect spatial relationship become apparent only in the generated image. Recent approaches introduce semantic or spatial guidance through textual reasoning and structural conditions [6, 8, 27, 28, 37]. However, specifying the intended composition does not necessarily instantiate its fine-grained geometry. As shown in Fig. 1(a), plan may specify woman holding ring without resolving the handring contact. The same bounding boxes allow different poses and depth orderings. Leaving these choices to the generator makes it difficult to verify the requested relationships or revise the geometry before synthesis. Geometry-aware approaches further explore explicit 3D scene planning and agentic revision, enabling more direct control over spatial relationships [4, 22]. While these methods primarily focus on textdriven image generation, multi-reference generation introduces an additional challenge: maintaining the correspondence between references and scene instances while transferring the planned composition into reference-faithful image synthesis. Executable scene code lets us inspect spatial relationships in the resulting geometry and rendered views and revise individual placements and poses before image synthesis. Drawing on these properties, we introduce MAGPIE, framework for multi-reference image generation through verifiable scene construction. MAGPIE constructs executable 3D proxies whose entities retain explicit bindings to the original visual references. As shown in Fig. 1(b), the agent executes each scene program, checks the geometry and rendered views against the requested relationships, and iteratively revises the program to correct discrepancies. The refined proxy rendering then guides composition, while the bound references provide each subjects appearance for the final image generator. Making verifiable scene construction useful for MRIG requires addressing two connected challenges. First, the agent must reliably construct and repair proxy that captures the composition specified by the references and instruction. Second, the generator must learn to follow the proxys structure while preserving appearance from the corresponding references. To address the first challenge, we develop structured agentic harness that integrates scene planning, procedural Blender construction, and iterative geometric and visual revision. Parameterized components and shared interaction anchors provide controllable geometry for individual entities and their interactions. Because program can execute successfully while placing entities incorrectly, the harness checks entity visibility, camera-relative ordering, and designated contacts on the constructed geometry. multimodal reviewer complements these measurements by examining the rendering against the references and instruction, and the agent uses the combined feedback to revise the scene. To address the second challenge, pretrained generators must learn to use simplified proxy renderings as structural guidance without copying their placeholder appearances. However, existing MRIG datasets generally lack supervision that aligns executable scene proxies with visual references and target images. We therefore construct MAGPIE-Instruct-3K, dataset of 3187 examples comprising reference images, instructions, executable Blender programs, proxy renderings, and target images. Through lightweight fine-tuning, pretrained generators learn to follow the proxys composition while preserving the appearance of the corresponding reference subjects. and SconeEval on DreamOmni2 demonstrate improvements in overall scores with both Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 and FLUX.2-klein-base-9B. On DreamOmni2, MAGPIE raises the FLUX backbones overall score from 38.87% to 67.08%, and outperforms ordinary fine-tuning on the same referencetarget pairs by 18.18 percentage points. The Qwen backbone likewise benefits beyond ordinary fine-tuning. These results support combining explicit scene construction with proxy-guided adaptation to improve reference-grounded image synthesis.

sections.title: Experiments
sections.content: Our contributions are threefold: We propose MAGPIE, framework that instantiates reference-associated scene relationships in executable proxies for inspection and correction before appearance synthesis. We develop structured harness for proxy construction and revision, and construct MAGPIE-Instruct-3K to teach generators to combine proxy structure with referencespecific appearance. We demonstrate improvements across two backbones and two benchmarks, including gains beyond ordinary generator fine-tuning. 2. Related Work 2.1. Multi-Reference Image Generation Unlike conventional text-to-image generation [5, 11, 20, 29], multi-reference image generation allows users to com2 Figure 2. Overview of MAGPIE. The coding harness converts reference images and an instruction into an executable proxy scene through planning, procedural construction, and geometric and visual refinement. The generator combines the proxys structure with referencespecific appearance. MAGPIE-Instruct-3K supports lightweight adaptation to this conditioning. bine subjects and visual attributes drawn from different reference images following textual instructions [3, 16, 32, 33]. DreamOmni2 [35] supports generation and editing with references to concrete subjects and abstract attributes, while Scone [30] distinguishes requested subjects from distractors. AutoRef [19] further explores agentic generation by automatically optimizing the harness for reference processing, image synthesis, and output selection. central challenge is preserving reference-specific appearance while arranging the selected subjects as instructed. This becomes more demanding when an instruction calls for multiple instances of the same subject. Each instance must retain the subjects appearance while being placed and posed according to the instruction. 2.2. Structural Control for Image Generation Structured planning expresses compositional intent through semantic descriptions and spatial conditions. Textual reasoning in Re-Align [8] clarifies target-scene content and reference associations, while layout-based approaches such as LayoutGPT [6] and LLM-grounded Diffusion [15] specify object placement. In reference-conditioned generation, ContextGen [37] and ConsistCompose [27] further associate subject identities with regions or coordinates. Richer conditions in ControlNet [41] and SeeThrough3D [1] extend control to pose, depth, viewpoint, and occlusion. These approaches provide increasingly detailed structural guidance, but such guidance alone does not establish that all requested relations are jointly realized. Verifying the composition and localizing necessary revisions before final synthesis remains challenging. 2.3. Executable Scene Representations Executable scene code allows composition to be rendered, checked against its specification, and revised before final image synthesis. Existing approaches explore procedural scenes and programmatic sketches, as in SceneCraft [9], CoCo [14] and GenClaw [39], or editable 3D scenes and layout refinement, as in MUSES [4], 3D Scratchpad [25], and SpatialGuard [22]. These methods primarily address text-driven scene construction, leaving the integration of user-provided subject identities into executable scenes less explored. To address this gap, MAGPIE grounds executable scene entities in the supplied references, enabling composition verification and revision while preserving referencespecific appearance in the final synthesis. 3. Method Given reference images = {I1, . . . , IN } and an instruction p, MAGPIE generates an image that preserves reference-specific appearances while satisfying the requested composition. As illustrated in Fig. 2, multimodal coding harness first constructs and refines an executable Blender scene specifying entity selection, instance counts, spatial arrangement, and interactions. The image generator 3 then uses the proxy rendering for structure and the original references for appearance, with explicit bindings between reference subjects and scene entities. We detail these stages below, followed by MAGPIE-Instruct-3K and lightweight adaptation for proxy-guided synthesis. 3.1. Agentic Proxy Scene Construction To instantiate the intended composition before image synthesis, we develop multimodal coding harness that translates reference images and instructions into executable Blender scenes. The harness integrates reference-grounded scene planning, constrained procedural construction, and render-guided refinement, producing structural proxy that captures the target entities and their spatial organization without requiring precise appearance reconstruction. Reference-Grounded Scene Planning. The coding agent selects the requested subjects from the references and creates an instance-level scene specification with entity counts, spatial and interaction relationships, and camera configuration. Each entity has unique identifier, reference associations, an approximate layout and pose, and proxy category for procedural modeling. relational graph encodes relative positioning, containment, support, and physical contact. We validate entity identifiers, reference associations, and relational endpoints before construction. Because the specification describes individual instances, it supports selective subject inclusion and multiple instances of the same reference subject with distinct compositional roles. Constrained Procedural Scene Construction. Based on the scene specification, the coding agent generates Blender program that instantiates the required entities and configures their geometry, placement, and camera viewpoint. To improve scene construction efficiency, we maintain reusable library of parameterized procedural modeling functions covering common entity categories, including articulated figures, animals, and structured objects. Each function exposes controllable parameters for geometry, scale, orientation, and pose. For entities not covered by the library, the agent constructs new procedural components using geometric primitives or custom meshes, which are subsequently incorporated into for reuse in future scene construction. Guided by the assigned proxy categories, the agent generates an individual builder for each entity, together with shared scene configuration. For entities covered by the library, each builder is required to invoke its designated procedural function. Before execution, we perform AST-based validation to ensure that all required builders are present and comply with their corresponding modeling interfaces. Independently constructed entities must also interact coherently. The components therefore use stable entityspecific mesh identifiers and shared world-space anchors to align interacting parts, such as hand with an objects grasping region or seated character with supporting surface. Geometric feasibility checks, including articulatedlimb reachability, identify inconsistent configurations during construction. Executing and rendering the program produces an initial proxy, while the mesh identifiers and anchors allow subsequent checks and revisions to target individual entities and interactions. Geometry and Vision Guided Refinement. Although the initial program instantiates the planned scene, its rendered composition may still contain errors in entity visibility, spatial arrangement, or physical interactions. We therefore introduce render guided refinement loop that combines geometric verification with multimodal visual review to identify discrepancies and guide code revision. The geometric verifier examines the executed Blender meshes to assess whether the constructed scene satisfies the specified structural constraints. It first checks the presence and visibility of planned entities through mesh identifiers, projected bounding boxes, and ray-based visibility estimation. Camera-relative spatial relationships are then examined using projected positions and depth ordering to detect incorrect left-right or front-back arrangements. For interactions involving physical contact, the verifier evaluates surface distances between designated mesh components and checks the visibility of relevant contact regions. These measurements provide localized feedback on geometric inconsistencies in the rendered composition. To detect semantic errors beyond these geometric measurements, multimodal reviewer examines the proxy rendering and localized crops alongside the references, instruction, scene specification, and geometric feedback. It checks entity inventory, reference associations, relative placement, poses, and interactions. At round k, let c(k) denote the Blender program, M(k) its executed meshes, and D(k) its rendering. The refinement loop is g(k) = Geom(S, M(k), D(k)), (k) = Review(I, p, S, D(k), g(k)), c(k+1) = Revise(c(k), g(k), (k)), D(k+1) = Render(c(k+1)), (1) where g(k) and (k) are geometric and visual feedback, respectively. The agent uses both to revise geometry, placement, interaction anchors, and camera configuration; the resulting rendering is evaluated in the next round. The harness retains the best candidate according to the verification results and performs at most six refinement rounds, stopping early when all verification criteria are satisfied. 4 Figure 3. Overview of MAGPIE-Instruct-3K. Across five compositional tasks, the dataset pairs reference images and instructions with proxy renderings and target images to teach generators to follow the proxys structure while preserving reference-specific appearance. Cross-Example Harness Refinement. Instance-level revision corrects individual scenes; recurring errors also inform offline improvements to the harness. We construct proxies for over 200 randomly sampled training examples and compare their renderings with the corresponding target images. Common failure patterns guide changes to scene planning and code generation to improve initial proxy quality and reduce repeated repairs. Target images are used for this offline development; at inference, the harness receives only the references and instruction. 3.2. Proxy-Guided Reference-Grounded Synthesis Building upon the proxy scene constructed in the preceding stage, we use its final rendering to provide explicit structural guidance for reference-grounded image synthesis. The proxy specifies entity arrangement, approximate geometry, poses, and interactions, while the original references supply identity and appearance details. We combine these inputs through ˆY = Gθ+θ(I, D, p), (2) where ˆY is the generated image, is the image generator, and θ and θ denote its pretrained parameters and LoRA updates, respectively. The proxy-aware prompt is derived from the instruction and the reference-to-entity bindings. It assigns each input its role: follow the proxys placement, poses, and spatial relationships; preserve each subjects appearance from its bound reference; and avoid reproducing the proxys simplified materials and colors. 3.3. MAGPIE-Instruct-3K and Model Adaptation Although proxy renderings provide explicit structural guidance, pretrained image generators may not interpret them as compositional constraints. As shown in Tab. 3, introducing proxy guidance into Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 without adaptation substantially degrades generation quality, motivating adaptation to this form of structural conditioning. However, existing multi-reference generation datasets generally lack paired executable proxy scenes and target images. We therefore construct MAGPIE-Instruct-3K using the scene construction harness. Source examples come primarily from Echo-4o [38] and the Scone [30] training set, supplemented by Pico-Banana [21], MICo-150K [31], and other public multi-reference generation datasets. Source details are provided in the supplementary material. We retain examples with identifiable entities and requirements expressible through proxy geometry, such as shape, poses and spatial arrangements. During construction, the coding agent receives the target image to align the proxy with the intended composition. We then use Qwen3.8-27B [24] as multimodal judge to filter proxytarget pairs based on entity inclusion and counts, spatial arrangements, poses and interactions, and framing and visibility. The evaluation prompt appears in the supplementary Material. The dataset contains 3187 examples, each comprising references, an instruction, an executable Blender program, proxy rendering, and target image. Fig. 3 presents the source and task distributions, representative examples, and the proxy-aware prompt template. Using this dataset, we adapt pretrained image generators through lightweight low-rank adaptation (LoRA), enabling them to leverage proxy-based structural guidance while preserving reference-specific appearances. Experiments We evaluate MAGPIE with two image generation backbones on multi-reference generation and editing benchmarks, then examine the contributions of generator adaptation, scene representation, and proxy refinement. 4.1. Experimental Setting Training. We adapted Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 [32] and FLUX.2 [klein] [12], referred to as Qwen and FLUX, respectively, on the 3187 examples in MAGPIE-Instruct-3K. We used Qwen3.8-flash [23] for agentic scene construction and visual review during both offline data construction and inference. We trained rank-32 LoRA adapters for five epochs with learning rate of 104 and batch size of one, using images up to 1024 1024 resolution. The pretrained generator parameters remained frozen. At inference, the agent receives only the references and instruction, and the harness performs at most six refinement rounds with early stopping, as described in Sec. 3.1. Evaluation. We evaluate on DreamOmni2 [35] and SconeEval [30] using their official evaluation scripts, scoring prompts, and aggregation procedures. DreamOmni2 covers generation and editing with concrete objects and abstract attributes. Its evaluation measures whether the output successfully satisfies the multimodal instruction; we report success rates for both categories, their aggregate within each task, and an overall score, all as percentages. SconeEval evaluates composition, distinction, and their combiincluding cross-category and intra-category subnation, Its composition score (COM) combines ject selection. prompt following and subject consistency through their perexample geometric mean. Its distinction score (DIS) averages subject-selection accuracy and F1, rescaled to the same 010 range. We report the benchmarks subtask scores and aggregate COM, DIS, and Overall, with higher values indicating better performance. 4.2. Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation Quantitative evaluation. On DreamOmni2, MAGPIE improves both generation and editing success with either backbone (Tab. 1). Qwen gains 22.25 percentage points in overall success over the original backbone. The gain is larger for FLUX, whose success rate rises from 38.87% to 67.08%, 28.21-point increase. Both variants outperform the strongest open-weight baseline, DreamOmni2 [35], and exceed the 61.44% overall success rate of the proprietary Gemini-2.5-Flash-Image. Ablation Study On SconeEval, MAGPIE improves both composition and subject distinction with either backbone (Tab. 2). With Effect of proxy-conditioned adaptation. We disentangle the effects of additional training data, inference-time proxy 7 Figure 4. Qualitative comparison of existing models on DreamOmni2 benchmark. guidance, and proxy-conditioned adaptation in Tab. 3. Standard SFT uses the same references, instructions, and target images as MAGPIE but excludes proxy renderings during both training and inference. It improves the overall score from 42.01% to 44.83% for Qwen and from 38.87% to 48.90% for FLUX, confirming that the training pairs themselves are beneficial. Conditioning on proxies during both adaptation and inference further raises the scores to 64.26% and 67.08%, outperforming standard SFT by 19.43 and 18.18 percentage points, respectively. In contrast, supplying the proxy only at inference without adaptation produces inconsistent effects: it substantially degrades Qwen to 29.47%, while improving FLUX to 46.08%. These results show that proxy renderings are not universally effective as zero-shot guidance; their structural benefit is realized most reliably when the generator is trained to interpret them. Effect of scene representation. We compare three representations of the scene plan (Tab. 4). Text Scene uses the entity-level plan produced by the first stage of the MAGPIE harness as textual guidance, while 2D Scene converts that plan into labeled bounding boxes. For each variant, we used this pipeline to construct training examples from MAGPIE-Instruct-3K and trained separate LoRA adapter for each backbone. At inference, the same pipeline produces the corresponding guidance from the input references and instruction. With rendered Blender proxy as guidance, 3D Scene achieves the highest aggregate generation score on both backbones (67.54%), exceeding the best alternative planning variant by 12.28 percentage points on Qwen and 8.77 on FLUX. Effect of proxy refinement. Using the adapted FLUX backbone, we evaluate generation and editing performance Figure 5. Generation and editing performance across refinement rounds. We visualize the progressive improvement in MAGPIEs aggregate generation and editing scores on DreamOmni2Bench across 0, 3, and 6 rounds of proxy refinement. by setting the maximum number of proxy refinement rounds to 0, 3, or 6. At zero rounds, the generator uses the initial proxy before render-guided refinement. Figure 5 reports DreamOmni2Bench scores for concrete and abstract examples in both generation and editing, along with the aggregate score for each task and the overall score. Both task aggregates rise across the three budgets, and the overall score increases from 53.61% at zero rounds to 67.08% at six rounds. The supplementary material also provides proxy construction reliability statistics, qualitative comparisons across refinement rounds, proxy quality assessments, and runtime analysis. 8 5. Conclusion In this work, we introduce MAGPIE, framework for multireference image generation that represents the requested composition as an executable 3D scene. coding agent arranges the selected subjects in this scene, checks its geometry and rendered view against the instruction, and revises the scene as needed. We also curate MAGPIE-Instruct-3K for lightweight fine-tuning so the generator learns to follow the refined rendering for composition and the original references for appearance. Experiments on DreamOmni2 and SconeEval show that MAGPIE improves overall performance with both Qwen and FLUX. We hope this work encourages further study of how executable scene representations can give users finer control over multi-reference image generation. 6. sections.title: Supplementary Material
sections.content: 7. Training Dataset Details MAGPIE-Instruct-3K contains 3,187 examples for proxyconditioned image generator adaptation, drawn from subject-driven generation, multi-reference composition, and reference-guided editing datasets. Construction comprises source selection, executable proxy construction, and structural filtering of proxytarget pairs. We describe these stages and the resulting task categories below. The corresponding prompt templates accompany the descriptions of each assessment stage. 7.1. Data Sources Echo-4o-Image. Echo-4o-Image [38] is GPT-4ogenerated dataset covering multi-reference generation, surreal fantasy generation, and complex instruction following. Its multi-reference subset pairs visual references and textual instructions with generated target images, supporting diverse reference-conditioned compositions. Scone-Train. Scone-Train [30] supports subject-driven generation in both single-candidate and multi-candidate settings. In the multi-candidate setting, each reference image may contain multiple candidate subjects, requiring the model to identify those specified by the instruction and compose them while preserving their identities. Pico-Banana via RCEdit. Pico-Banana-400K [21] provides image-editing triplets consisting of source image, an instruction, and an edited target. We use its referenceconditioned adaptation provided by RCEdit [40], which augments the original editing pairs with reference images and corresponding instructions. These examples specify editing requirements through both textual and visual conditions. MICo-150K. MICo-150K [31] supports multi-image composition across human-centric, object-centric, and humanobject It also includes Decomposition-and-Recomposition subset, in which complex images are decomposed into component references for subsequent recomposition. interaction tasks. OmniRef-training. OmniRef-training [10] supports generation conditioned on heterogeneous references that specify subjects, backgrounds, poses, lighting, and styles. Different reference images can therefore provide distinct types of guidance within the same example. MacroData. MacroData [2], introduced in MACRO, covers customization, illustration, spatial reasoning, and temporal prediction. Its customization component focuses on reference-based composition, while its spatial component addresses novel-view generation. UNO-1M. UNO-1M [34] provides image pairs constructed through an in-context generation pipeline. It emphasizes subject consistency across different contexts and includes captions and visual consistency annotations for subject-driven generation. 7.2. Data Selection for Proxy Construction We sample candidate examples from the source datasets and assess their suitability for proxy construction using Qwen3.8-27B, conditioned on the references, instruction, and target image. Selection focuses on whether the requested composition can be represented by identifiable entities and simplified geometry, including object shapes, instance counts, spatial arrangements, poses, and interactions. Accepted examples must provide clear reference-to-subject correspondence and sufficient visible evidence to assess the relevant structural requirements. Appearance-only transformations, such as texture or style changes without meaningful geometric requirement, are excluded. Mixed requirements remain eligible when their structural component can be expressed by proxy. We also check the target for evident conflicts with the instruction or referenced subjects, ensuring that it provides usable composition target for construction. Figure 6 gives the selection prompt. 7.3. Proxy Construction and Pair Filtering For each selected example, the scene construction harness produces an executable Blender program and proxy rendering. During this stage, the coding agent receives the target image alongside the references and instruction to align the proxy with the training composition. Target images are used only during dataset construction; at inference, the harness receives only the references and instruction. We then assess proxytarget consistency using Qwen3.827B along four dimensions: entity inclusion and counts, 1 Prompt 1: Source Example Selection Role. You assess whether an image-generation example is suitable for constructing simplified 3D proxy scene. Input. Reference images, generation or editing instruction, and target image. The target is construction reference and must itself be checked for consistency. Task. Determine whether the example contains clear structural composition that can be represented by coarse geometry and evaluated in rendered view. Selection Criteria. 1. Identifiable subjects. The subjects required by the instruction can be identified and associated with the relevant references. Additional candidate subjects in reference are allowed when the requested selection is unambiguous. 2. Geometric relevance. The example contains meaningful requirement involving shape, instance count, spatial arrangement, pose, support, containment, or contact. simplified proxy should be able to express this requirement without reproducing detailed textures or materials. 3. Valid target. The target depicts the requested subjects and composition without clear contradictions in identity, count, or the required relationships. 4. Observable structure. The target provides sufficient evidence to assess the relevant arrangement, pose, or interaction. Reject cases where essential evidence is unavailable because of ambiguity or severe occlusion. Decision Rules. Accept only when all four criteria are satisfied. Reject appearance-only transformations without meaningful structural requirement. Do not reject sample merely because it also includes appearance conditions or requires complex geometry. Judge representability, not ease of construction. Do not invent hidden objects, contacts, or poses; mark criterion as false when the available evidence is insufficient. Output Format. Return raw JSON only. Each criterion is Boolean; accept is true only when all four are true. Provide short evidence-based reason. { } "identifiable_subjects": true, "geometric_relevance": true, "valid_target": true, "observable_structure": true, "accept": true, "reason": "Brief evidence supporting the decision." Figure 6. Prompt template for selecting source examples suitable for executable proxy construction. The assessment uses the references, instruction, and target image before proxy is constructed. spatial arrangements, poses and interactions, and framing and visibility. The assessment checks whether the proxy provides structural guidance consistent with the target, while allowing coarse shapes and simplified articulation. Differences in texture, color, material, and other appearance details are excluded. Figure 7 provides the filtering prompt. Each retained example comprises reference images, an instruction, an executable Blender program, proxy rendering, and target image. 7.4. Data Categorization We organize the retained examples into five categories according to their principal compositional requirement: Shape Alignment, concerning coarse object form and proportions; Object Interaction, concerning actions and functional relationships between entities, including humanhuman and humanobject interactions; Spatial Arrangement, concerning relative positions, depth ordering, and spatial containment; Scene Composition, concerning subject selection, instance counts, and the assembly of subjects and backgrounds; and Pose Control, concerning subjects posture and articulated configuration. Although instructions may combine several requirements, each example receives one primary category based on its dominant requested operation. Reference and target images are used to resolve visual referents. Object Interaction concerns how entities act together, whereas Pose Control concerns an individual subjects configuration and Spatial Arrangement concerns relative placement. Figure 8 presents the categorization prompt. We manually inspect the 338 examples flagged as ambiguous and assign their final labels using the same category definitions. 8. Implementation Details We implement generator adaptation using DiffSynth-Studio and Hugging Face Accelerate. For Qwen-Image-Edit2511 and FLUX.2-klein-base-9B, we train rank-32 LoRA 2 Prompt 2: ProxyTarget Pair Filtering Role. You assess whether simplified proxy rendering provides reliable structural guidance for its paired target image. Input. Reference images, generation or editing instruction, target image, and proxy rendering. The references identify the requested subjects, the instruction specifies the requirements, and the target depicts the composition to be matched. Task. Evaluate structural agreement between the proxy and target with respect to the requested composition. Evaluation Criteria. 1. Entity inclusion and counts. The proxy contains the required subject instances with the correct counts. Reject missing, duplicated, or additional task-relevant instances. 2. Spatial arrangements. Relative positions, depth ordering, orientation, and scale agree with the target where they affect the requested composition. Check left/right, above/below, front/behind, and containment when applicable. 3. Poses and interactions. Task-relevant body configurations, object orientations, and interactions agree with the target. Check required grasping, support, contact, and containment relations; mere proximity is insufficient when contact is required. 4. Framing and visibility. The proxy preserves the compositionally relevant framing and subject visibility. Reject occlusion, or viewpoint differences that hide required instances or substantially change the intended composition. Evaluation Boundaries. Allow coarse geometry and simplified articulation when the required structure remains clear. Ignore differences in color, texture, material, lighting, facial detail, and rendering realism. Do not require pixel-level alignment or exact background reconstruction. Assess only visible evidence; do not assume that hidden relation is correct. Decision Rules. Assign each criterion pass, fail, or uncertain. criterion passes when its applicable requirements are satisfied; it also passes if no such requirement applies. Use uncertain when required property cannot be assessed from the inputs. Accept only when all four criteria pass. Output Format. Return raw JSON only, with short explanation identifying the decisive agreement, mismatch, or missing evidence. { } "entities_and_counts": "pass", "spatial_arrangement": "pass", "pose_and_interaction": "pass", "framing_and_visibility": "pass", "accept": true, "reason": "Brief evidence supporting the decision." Figure 7. Prompt template for filtering proxytarget pairs by structural consistency. Appearance differences caused by the simplified proxy representation are excluded from the assessment. adapters in the diffusion transformer while keeping the pretrained parameters frozen. Both models are trained for five epochs on the 3,187 examples in MAGPIE-Instruct-3K using AdamW with learning rate of 104 and weight decay of 0.01. Training uses eight H800 GPUs with per-GPU batch size of one and no gradient accumulation. For square images, the pixel budget is capped at 1048576 pixels (1024 1024). Gradient checkpointing is enabled for both generators; Qwen additionally uses activation offloading during gradient checkpointing. 9. More Details in the Harness This section details verification and candidate selection within the MAGPIE harness. single agent orchestrates scene planning, construction, verification, and revision. The scene specification defines entity identifiers and reference associations, required relations, and framing requirements. Geometric checks use measurements from the executed Blender meshes and camera, while visual review uses the agents assessment of rendered views against the references and instruction. These checks provide revision feedback, and the harness programmatically applies the acceptance and candidate-retention rules to their outputs. Geometric and visual evidence. Table 5 specifies the geometric tests, their thresholds, and their applicability. Entity identifiers associate measurements with the intended instances and contact parts. The agent receives the proxy render, localized relation views, references, instruction, scene specification, and geometric feedback. It describes the observed composition, identifies structures to preserve and defects to repair, and returns pass, minor, fail, or uncertain judgments with visual evidence. valid review must follow this structured schema and provide nonempty evidence. Contact assessment combines the distance test with visual assessment of the requested pose and 3 Table 5. Operational constraints for proxy verification. Tests apply to the entities and relations declared in the scene specification. Image coordinates are normalized to [0, 1]. Entity visibility measures occlusion by other entities, whereas exact-part visibility distinguishes individual meshes. Visual review complements these approximate geometric diagnostics. Constraint Operational rule Inventory and ownership Surface contact Framing Entity visibility Projected readability Interaction visibility Relative ordering Visual requirements Each planned entity has at least one executed mesh with its entity_id_ prefix. Declared contact endpoints must map to meshes of the specified subject and target. For touch, hold, support, and wear, sample vertex-to-surface distances in both directions using bounding volume hierarchies (BVHs). The minimum sampled distance must satisfy (cid:98)d τ , with τ = max{105, 0.025L, min(2p, 0.15L)}. Here is the smaller world-space bounding-box diagonal and is the camera-derived world-space size of one render pixel at the contact. For each frame-required entity, the union of projected mesh bounds must lie within [0.015, 1.015]2, and no mesh vertex may lie behind the camera. Cast 2020 ray grid over the clipped projected bounding box. Among rays hitting the entity in isolation, the fraction whose first full-scene hit belongs to that entity must be at least 0.55 for humans and 0.28 otherwise. Named head meshes, when present, receive an additional test with thresholds 0.70 and 0.35, respectively. Any part of the same entity counts as visible, including for head tests; zero-hit tests fail. Frame-required entities tagged as humans, animals, or birds must occupy at least 0.20, 0.13, or 0.045 of image height, respectively, using clipped projected bounds. Contact meshes named as hand, handle, shaft, or glasses bridge require exact-part visibility of at least 0.22: the first scene hit must be that mesh. Nonhuman entities participating in hold require entity visibility of at least 0.65. Left/right relations require strictly positive signed displacement between projected bounding-box centers in the requested direction. Front/behind relations use strictly positive camera-depth difference. No additional positive margin is imposed; above and inside are assessed visually. Critical checks and every declared relation require pass. For other applicable checks, fail and uncertain count as failures, while minor is tolerated. The critical checks and candidate-level aggregation are defined in the text. interaction. candidate are Visual decision rules. Critical checks include entity inventory, reference binding, spatial layout, pose/contact, and source preservation for editing. These checks and every declared relation must receive pass; minor, fail, or uncertain label on any of them counts as visual failure. Source preservation is inapplicable to generation and treated as satisfied. For other checks and applicable requirements, fail and uncertain count as failures, while minor is tolerated. Appearance-only requirements may be inapplicable to structural proxy, and its neutral colors and materials are allowed. Acceptance and candidate retention. For successfully rendered candidate c(k) with valid visual review, let Gk and Vk count failed geometric and visual diagnostic records, respectively. The channels are recorded separately: defect detected by both contributes to both counts. Let Mk count minor labels among fixed visual checks and applicable requirements; relation labels enter Vk. The score and retained sk = (Gk + Vk, Gk, Mk, k), = lex arg min kK sk, (4) where contains the iteration indices of valid reviewed candidates; the retained code and render correspond to k. Lexicographic ordering prioritizes fewer total failures, then fewer geometric failures, then fewer minor judgments. If these three counts tie, the earlier candidate is retained. Geometric failures therefore have priority when total failure counts tie. Runtime acceptance requires Gk = Vk = 0, so neither visual pass nor geometric pass alone establishes acceptance. tolerated minor judgment does not prevent it. Revision and stopping. Each revision starts from the retained code and render with their corresponding feedback. Feedback from rejected proposal remains associated with that proposal. The agent is instructed to preserve satisfied relations while repairing identified defects; each revised program is executed, rendered, and reviewed again. Under the default budget, the harness performs at most six refinement rounds and stops early when Gk = Vk = 0. At Prompt 3: Data Categorization Role. You categorize training examples by their principal compositional requirement. Input. Reference images, generation or editing instruction, and target image. Task. Assign one primary category based on the instruction. Use the images to resolve visual references, without treating incidental image content as requirement. Categories. 1. Shape Alignment. Matching or changing coarse object shape, silhouette, or proportions. Excludes appearance-only changes and articulated body posture. 2. Object Interaction. Actions and functional relationships between entities, including humanhuman and humanobject interactions. The main requirement concerns how entities act together, or how one uses, manipulates, or responds to another. 3. Spatial Arrangement. Relative placement, depth ordering, distance, or spatial containment. The main requirement concerns where entities are located relative to one another. 4. Scene Composition. Selecting subjects, specifying instance counts, or combining subjects and backgrounds into scene, when no other category is the dominant requirement. 5. Pose Control. Specifying or transferring subjects body posture or articulated configuration. The posture itself is the main requirement, rather than an action involving another entity. Assignment Rules. Identify the main requested operation and distinguish it from supporting constraints. Choose the category whose violation would most directly defeat that operation. Distinguish actions between entities from individual postures and relative placement. Multiple subjects, physical proximity, or incidental contact alone do not establish an interaction. If categories remain equally central, or none is supported, return null and set needs_review to true. Do not force labels to match desired distribution. Output Format. Return raw JSON only. Use an exact category name from the list, or null, and briefly identify the decisive instruction requirement. The following illustrates the output format only. { } "primary_category": "Pose Control", "needs_review": false, "reason": "Posture is the main request." Figure 8. Prompt template for categorizing examples by their principal compositional requirement. the budget limit, it returns the retained candidate, marked needs_review if failures remain. Invalid submissions, failed renders, and malformed reviews do not replace the retained candidate; if the budget is exhausted without valid reviewed render, construction returns an error. Diagnostics, visual evidence, selection scores, and retainedcandidate identifiers are logged together, linking each retention decision to its supporting evidence. 10. Additional Evaluation Analysis We analyze the computation required for scene construction, compare against additional sampling under comparable time budgets, and examine how refinement affects generation quality. We then assess the structural quality of the selected proxies through human evaluation. 10.1. Inference Time Analysis includes code generation and Blender execution and rendering up to the first successful proxy, including preceding unsuccessful attempts. Refinement includes proxy verification, subsequent code revisions, and the corresponding Blender execution and re-rendering. Each recorded operation is assigned to exactly one stage. Uninstrumented input processing, validation outside these calls, and orchestration are excluded. The timing analysis aggregates recorded model calls and Blender executions within the first six construction cycles, including timed retries, failed attempts, and timeouts; subsequent cycles are excluded. Construction statistics cover all 319 DreamOmni2Bench examples and 409 SconeEval examples, all of which produced successful renders. Two annotators independently reviewed 319 final proxy renderings returned by the harness (Sec. 9) on DreamOmni2Bench, covering 164 abstract editing, 41 concrete editing, 90 abstract generation, and 24 concrete generation examples. They inspected the references, instruction, and selected proxy for entity inclusion and counts, spatial arrangements, poses and interactions, and framing and visibility. Appearance differences inherent to simplified proxy geometry were excluded. Each proxy receives one overall label: correct, when the requested composition is satisfied; minor issue, when localized discrepancy does not substantially alter it; or major error, when an essential structural requirement is violated. Table 9 reports the final label distributions within each task group and Cohens κ computed from independent annotations before disagreement resolution. Across the audited examples, 292 (91.54%) are correct, 25 (7.84%) contain minor issues, and two (0.63%) contain major errors. Abstract generation has the lowest correctness rate (86.67%) and accounts for both major errors. The other groups have correctness rates of 92.07%100.00%, with no major errors observed. Available inter-annotator agreement values range from κ = 0.787 to 0.854. These results indicate that most selected proxies preserve the requested composition, while abstract generation remains the most errorprone audited group. 11. Additional Qualitative Results 11.1.
